p: You walk into an imperial hall at the foot of the Palatine and find it painted from floor to ceiling, layer over layer: this is the oldest Christian monument in the Roman Forum. The building was Roman first, a vestibule to the palace ramps of Domitian's time, and in the 6th century it became a church. For about three hundred years painters kept adding to it, so one wall can carry three or four campaigns of saints and Madonnas on top of each other.

The church survived because it was buried. An earthquake in 847 brought the Palatine slopes down on it, the clergy moved to Santa Maria Nova (today Santa Francesca Romana), and a later church was even built on top of the ruins in 1617. It was removed when excavators found the old church in 1900. After that the site was closed for most of the twentieth century; it reopened in 2016 after a long conservation programme.

The thing to find is the "palimpsest wall" next to the apse, where you can count the layers like strata in a rock face. Byzantine-trained painters worked here in the 7th and 8th centuries, when Rome was still governed from Constantinople, and the church is one of the best places anywhere to see what Greek-style painting looked like in the West before the year 800.

Practical: it is a "SUPER site" of the Parco del Colosseo, so the base Forum ticket does not get you in; book the Full Experience ticket. Ministry hours were 9:30–18:00 daily in 2026, but SUPER sites close on free first Sundays.
s-maria-antiqua.s: Ministero della Cultura (Parco archeologico del Colosseo); fororomano.org; Wikipedia

p: Look at the side walls before you go in: Ionic and Tuscan columns of real Roman temples stick out of the masonry. San Nicola was built in the middle of the Forum Holitorium, the old vegetable market by the Tiber, on top of three temples of the 3rd–2nd century BC (usually named for Janus, Spes and Juno Sospita). The church used the middle temple as its core and simply walled in the columns of the other two.

The name "in Carcere" (in prison) is a medieval mistake. The vaulted rooms in the podium, really shops or storerooms, were taken in the 14th century for the Tullianum prison. Giacomo della Porta finished the façade in 1599, so the outside is a Counter-Reformation front pressed against Republican stonework.

Downstairs is the real treat: a small ticket takes you into the podiums, where you walk in narrow passages between the foundations of the three temples. It is one of the clearest places in Rome to see how a medieval church literally ate the buildings it replaced. Inside, look for the 10th-century inscription on the first column of the right aisle.
Practical: daily except Wednesday, 10:00–17:00 (rome-roma.net, checked May 2026). Guided underground visits also run through local associations.

San Clemente is the famous one, and it earns it: you go down through three Romes in twenty minutes. At street level is a 12th-century basilica with a gold apse mosaic of the Cross as a tree of life. Under it is the 4th-century church it replaced, and under that a 1st-century Roman building with a sanctuary of Mithras, the soldiers' god, still with its stone benches and altar. At the bottom you hear water: an ancient channel still runs through the foundations.

The Irish Dominicans who run the church began digging in 1857 and found the lower basilica almost intact, filled with rubble by the builders of 1100. Its frescoes are among the earliest medieval paintings in Rome.

The clue to find is the Sisinnius fresco in the lower church: a pagan prefect orders his servants to drag off a column, and the painted speech bubbles include rough early Italian ("fili de le pute, traite" – roughly "pull, you sons of whores"). It is one of the first written traces of the Italian language, and it is a curse.
Practical: timed tickets, best bought online; photos are not allowed below. A short walk from the Colosseum, and a good first stop before Santi Quattro Coronati.
s-clemente.s: Basilica di San Clemente; Google Places (hours, 2026); visitor reports

p: Step in and you are inside a ring of columns under a timber roof, more like a tent than a church. Santo Stefano is the oldest and best-preserved centrally planned church in Rome, built in the late 5th century; coins of Libius Severus (461–465) were found in its foundations, and dendrochronology dates the roof timber to about 455. Its round, cross-in-circle plan copies the Holy Sepulchre in Jerusalem.

The walls are the reason most people remember it. In 1582 Niccolò Pomarancio and Matteo da Siena painted 34 scenes of martyrdom around the ambulatory for the Jesuit college that trained missionaries: boiling, flaying, crushing, each panel lettered A, B, C and keyed to captions in Latin and Italian. It is a field guide to what the students might face. Dickens was among the visitors it disturbed.

The church sits on top of the Castra Peregrinorum, the barracks of soldiers on detached duty (often described as the emperors' intelligence service), and a Mithraeum lies below it. Look also for the marble chair said to be Gregory the Great's, cut from an ancient seat.
Practical: closed Monday; hours vary by source, so check before going. The Mithraeum is closed.
s-stefano-rotondo.s: Cathopedia; Churches of Rome Wiki; idealista (Aug 2026); lechiesediroma.info

p: Under the basilica of Santi Giovanni e Paolo, entered from the sloping Clivo di Scauro, is a whole block of Roman houses from the 2nd to the 4th century: twenty-odd rooms on several levels, many still painted. It is the best place in Rome to see the step between a Roman home and a church, because here a Christian confessio, a little shrine with martyrdom scenes, was painted right into a stairwell of the house.

Tradition says this was the home of two officials, John and Paul, martyred under Julian the Apostate in the 360s, and that the basilica was built over their graves. The excavations, begun by a Passionist priest in 1887, found a house that had been rebuilt and repainted for centuries, including pagan scenes next to Christian ones.

The clue is the confessio on the stair landing: a small niche with figures praying and a scene of arrest. Visitors complain the English captions are poor, so read up before you go, and download any guide first: there is no mobile signal underground.

marcellino-pietro.t: Catacombs of Saints Marcellinus and Peter + Mausoleum of Helena
p: Out on the Via Casilina, beside the traffic of Tor Pignattara, stands the broken drum of a huge imperial tomb: the mausoleum Constantine built, probably first for himself, then for his mother Helena. Behind it lies one of the most richly painted catacombs in Rome, with about 18,000 m² of galleries and something like 15,000 burials in the 3rd century alone.

The catacomb is named for two martyrs of the Diocletian persecution, a priest and an exorcist. Constantine built a circus-shaped basilica over it and the mausoleum against it, so this is one of the first places where an emperor attached his own dynasty to a Christian cemetery. The frescoes, restored in the 2000s with laser cleaning, include banquets, Bible scenes and a rare Christ between Peter and Paul.

The clue is in the name of the district: Tor Pignattara means "tower of the pots". The mausoleum's vault was lightened with clay amphorae (pignatte) built into the concrete, a classic Roman trick. Look for them in the broken dome.
Practical: the catacomb is guided only and must be booked; tours run in the morning and afternoon. Visitors who turn up without booking are sometimes squeezed in.
marcellino-pietro.s: Pontificia Commissione di Archeologia Sacra (catacombeditalia.va); santimarcellinoepietro.it; Ministero della Cultura

p: The Tiber island has been about healing for 2,300 years. In 291 BC Rome brought the cult of Asclepius here during a plague, and the island still holds a hospital (Fatebenefratelli). San Bartolomeo was built over the temple site in 998 by Emperor Otto III, and its Romanesque bell tower dates from the 12th century.

Find three things. On the steps up to the altar is a marble well-head cut from an ancient column drum, its rim worn by bucket chains; it stands over the old sacred spring. On the left wall of the chapel of the Virgin is a 14 cm cannonball, fired by the French from the Via Aurelia in June 1849 while they besieged the Roman Republic; it broke through the front wall and stopped on the altar, and a Latin inscription records that the friars were spared. And behind a grille is a 10th–11th-century Arab bronze basin.
Since 2000 the church has also been the memorial of the "new martyrs" of the 20th and 21st centuries, with objects left by people killed under Nazism, Communism and in mission countries.
s-bartolomeo-isola.s: romasegreta.it; Churches of Rome Wiki; Cathopedia; cosafarearoma.org

p: In an unpromising corner of Magliana, by the river, stands a small medieval church on a three-level stack: a late-13th-century church on top, a crypt from about the 7th century in the middle, and a 2nd–3rd-century Roman tomb chamber at the bottom with traces of painting. It began as a pagan funerary monument along a road and has been reused ever since.
The name is a corruption. The crypt held relics of two Egyptian saints, Cyrus and John; "Abbas Cyrus" became "Abbaciro", then "Pacera", then "Passera". There is no Saint Passera.

Across the road is Santo Volto di Gesù (2006), so this is the best pair in Rome for the whole church story in one stop: a Roman tomb turned into a church, and a 21st-century church by Sartogo and Grenon facing it.
Practical: the church is usually closed; the parish of Santo Volto opens it for Sunday Mass, and local associations run occasional guided visits to the lower levels.

aracoeli-column.t: Santa Maria in Aracoeli: the drilled column
p: Santa Maria in Aracoeli stands on the highest point of the Capitol, at the top of a steep marble stair built in 1348 in thanks for the end of the Black Death. Inside, the nave is carried by ancient columns of different heights and stones, taken from ruined buildings. It was the city's civic church for centuries, where Rome's government met and celebrated.

The clue: count to the third column on the left. It has a hole bored clean through it, about 74 cm long and 3 cm wide, at head height. The traditional story makes it an astronomical device for sighting the sun. In 2014 the astronomer Costantino Sigismondi measured it (axis at azimuth 116°, altitude 17.3°) and concluded that it "was probably not used for meridian observations", though since the column has been moved, its original use is open.

Look also for the Cosmatesque floors and the chapel of the Santo Bambino, a carved wooden Christ Child that Romans took to the sick; the original was stolen in 1994 and a copy is shown. Legend puts here the spot where the Sibyl showed Augustus a vision of the Virgin and Child: "the altar of heaven".

Walk into the courtyard of the old Sapienza university and look up at the end of it: the dome steps up in rings and ends in a spiral lantern that winds like a corkscrew into a crown of iron. Inside, the walls swing in and out so the whole room seems to move. Francesco Borromini built it in 1642–60 as the chapel of Rome's university, founded in 1303.

The plan is pure geometry: two overlapping triangles make a six-pointed star, and Borromini cut and rounded its points into alternating concave and convex walls. There is no separate dome on a drum; the wall simply rises into the vault, so your eye follows the lines from the floor to the lantern without a break. The church has been read as a bee (the Barberini family emblem), a star of Solomon and a symbol of Wisdom; Borromini left no explanation.
The clue: stand in the centre and follow one line of the floor pattern up the wall and into the dome. Outside, the spiral was struck by lightning four times in 32 years, Arte.it notes.
Practical: closed for years, it reopened on 27 October 2026 after a PNRR-funded restoration, free on weekday mornings. The building is the State Archive, so the courtyard gate is the way in.
s-ivo.s: Finestre sull'Arte (27 Oct 2026); SiViaggia; Arte.it; Google Places

p: Sant'Ignazio is the Jesuits' second great church in Rome, and the joke is in the roof. The dome was planned but never built, so in 1685 the painter and mathematician Andrea Pozzo painted a dome on a flat canvas about 17 m across. Stand on the marked disc in the nave and you see a drum, windows and a lantern; walk past the disc and the illusion bends and breaks. The present canvas may be a 19th-century replacement (sources conflict).

The nave vault is the bigger trick: Pozzo painted St Ignatius carried into heaven with the architecture of the church continuing upwards, so the ceiling seems twice as high as it is. It is applied projective geometry, and Pozzo wrote a textbook on perspective that architects used for a century.
The clue: find the two yellow marble discs in the nave floor, one for the vault and one for the dome, and stand on each. Look for the angel holding a concave mirror with the name of Jesus.
Science bonus: the church was built for the Collegio Romano next door, the Jesuit university where Angelo Secchi later ran his observatory on the piers meant for the dome (see Collegio Romano).

On elegant Via Giulia a façade carries winged skulls and the motto "Hodie mihi, cras tibi": today me, tomorrow you. This was the church of the Confraternity of Prayer and Death, founded in the 16th century to pull bodies out of the Tiber and collect the dead found in the countryside, people no one would bury. Between 1552 and 1896 they buried more than 8,000.

Ferdinando Fuga rebuilt the church on an oval plan in 1733–37. The cemetery behind it, which ran down to the river, was destroyed in the 1880s when the embankments of the Lungotevere were built; what is left is the crypt under the church, with altars, chandeliers and wall decorations made of bones.

The clue: read the skulls. Many have a date, the place where the body was found and the cause of death written on the forehead, so the room is also a 19th-century register of Roman accidents and drownings.
Practical: a PNRR restoration of the decoration was under way in 2026 and opening times conflict between sources. Treat the visit as "if open"; the façade is worth the stop anyway.
orazione-morte.s: Turismo Roma; Fanpage; Soprintendenza Speciale di Roma (PNRR project, 2026); it.wikipedia; America Magazine; map pin approximate

p: Near St Peter's is a hospital that has been working since the 12th century, on the site of an 8th-century hostel for English pilgrims (the Schola Saxonum, hence "in Sassia"). Pope Sixtus IV rebuilt it in 1473–78 around the Corsia Sistina, a single ward 120 m long, frescoed with the story of the hospital's founding and crowned by an octagonal chapel where Mass was said in sight of every bed.

The clue is on the street side: a marble wheel set in the wall, the ruota degli esposti. Parents could put a baby into the wheel, turn it and ring a bell; the child was taken in anonymously. Next to it is an alms slot. Under the portico, on the fourth pillar from the end, a plaque marks the height of the great flood of 1598.

The National Museum of the History of Medicine next door has anatomical models, surgical instruments and an apothecary with a grinder for quinine bark, which for a chemist may be the best stop on the whole map.
Practical: the Corsia and church are shown on booked visits; email well ahead.
s-spirito-sassia.s: monnoroma.it; Turismo Roma; Wikipedia (Museo Storico Nazionale dell'Arte Sanitaria)

p: In 527 Pope Felix IV turned a hall of Vespasian's Forum of Peace into a church, with the round "Temple of Romulus" on the Forum side as its vestibule. The apse mosaic, Christ on red clouds against a deep blue sky, is one of the oldest and most influential in Rome. The clue: at the back of the church a glass window looks straight into the round temple, and on the Forum side the temple still has its original Roman bronze doors.

San Crisogono was one of Rome's first parish churches. The church you see was rebuilt in 1123 and remodelled in 1626, with huge porphyry columns said to come from an ancient building; in 1907 the 4th-century church was found intact below it. The clue: go down through the sacristy and walk the old nave, with sarcophagi and early-medieval frescoes, while the trams run overhead.

Legend says this was Cecilia's house and that she survived three days in her own steam bath before being beheaded. Under the church are real Roman houses with a set of round basins, sometimes identified as a tannery or dye works, a nice chemistry question to settle on site. Upstairs, Stefano Maderno's marble Cecilia (1600) lies on her side with the wound visible, carved, it is said, as her body was found when the tomb was opened in 1599.

The Tullianum was Rome's only real prison, where enemies like Vercingetorix and the Catiline conspirators were held and strangled. Christian tradition puts Peter and Paul here and tells of a spring that rose so Peter could baptise his guards (legend). The clue: the hole in the floor of the upper room, the only way into the lower cell in antiquity. Visitors find the €10 ticket steep for a fifteen-minute visit.

Domitilla is one of the largest catacombs in Rome. You enter through the semi-underground basilica of Saints Nereus and Achilleus, built in the 4th century by cutting down into the cemetery, so the columns rise straight from the catacomb floor. That is the clue: a church you go down into.

s-sebastiano.t: San Sebastiano and the Memoria Apostolorum
p: Under San Sebastiano is the "triclia", a room where 3rd-century Christians met for funeral meals in honour of Peter and Paul, whose relics may have been kept here for a time. The walls are covered with hundreds of scratched invocations ("Petre et Paule, petite pro…"), among the oldest pilgrim graffiti anywhere. The clue is those scratches; see them on the catacomb tour.
s-sebastiano.s: Google Places; Churches of Rome Wiki (not checked on site); map pin approximate

p: Built about 350 for Constantia, daughter of Constantine, this is a round domed hall ringed by twelve pairs of granite columns. The ambulatory vault keeps its original mosaics: birds, vines and cupids treading grapes, pagan in look and Christian in meaning. It shows how the first Christian monuments borrowed Roman decoration. The porphyry sarcophagus is a copy; the original is in the Vatican Museums.

From outside, Santi Quattro Coronati looks like a castle, and that was the point: the Lateran palace was next door and the complex sheltered popes in troubled times. Augustinian nuns still live here. The clue: in the entrance court, ring at the wheel (rota) through which the enclosed nuns pass things; they let you into the Cappella di San Silvestro, painted in 1246 with Constantine's conversion, a piece of papal propaganda showing the emperor leading the pope's horse.

Pope Paschal I built Santa Prassede in 817 and added the tiny chapel of San Zeno as a tomb for his mother, Theodora: the only room in Rome fully covered in Byzantine-style gold mosaic. The clue: find Theodora with a square halo, the medieval sign that the person was still alive when the portrait was made. The chapel also holds a column fragment venerated as the column of the Flagellation (authenticity unknown).

The Baths of Diocletian had round towers at the corners of their enclosure; in 1598 Caterina Sforza Cesarini had one of them turned into this church. The coffered dome, lit only from an opening at the top, makes it a miniature Pantheon, and the acoustics are remarkable. It pairs with Santa Maria degli Angeli, the same baths turned church by Michelangelo, five minutes away.

vincenzo-anastasio.t: Santi Vincenzo e Anastasio a Trevi
p: While the crowds face the fountain, turn round. This was the parish of the Quirinal palace, and from Sixtus V (died 1590) to Leo XIII (died 1903) the praecordia, the heart and viscera removed for embalming, of 22 popes were brought here in urns. The clue: two marble plaques in the sanctuary list all 22 names. The façade (Martino Longhi the Younger, 1646–50, for Cardinal Mazarin) has so many columns that Romans called it "il Canneto", the reed bed.
vincenzo-anastasio.s: Walks in Rome; Wikipedia (list of extant papal tombs); Google Places

p: Under Santa Maria della Concezione on Via Veneto, the Capuchin friars arranged the bones of their dead brothers into arches, chandeliers and rosettes. A sign tells you: "What you are now, we once were; what we are now, you will be." It is the city's best-known ossuary and the obvious comparison for the smaller, stranger crypt of Santa Maria dell'Orazione e Morte. Hawthorne set a chapter of *The Marble Faun* here.
capuchin-crypt.s: Google Places; Hawthorne, The Marble Faun (ch. XXI)

p: In the courtyard of San Pietro in Montorio, Bramante built in about 1502 a tiny circular martyrium with Doric columns and a dome, on the traditional spot of Peter's crucifixion. It is the first building of the High Renaissance and the model for the dome of St Peter's. Go down to the crypt, where a beam of light falls on the spot. Sorrentino shot a scene of *La grande bellezza* in the cloister.

Before 1870 the popes did not allow Protestant churches inside the walls. As soon as Rome became Italy's capital, the American Episcopalians built this striped Gothic church on Via Nazionale (G. E. Street, 1873–80). The clue: in Edward Burne-Jones's apse mosaics, look for the saints with famous faces: Lincoln, Garibaldi and Grant are said to be among them.

From the street the dome shines like metal, because it is: San Gioacchino's octagonal dome was clad in aluminium in 1897, when aluminium was still a new, expensive metal. Inside, its blue surface is pierced with six-pointed stars of coloured glass that glow when the sun is on them. The local site romamia claims it is the oldest aluminium building element in Rome still in use.

The church was built in 1891–98 (finished 1911) by Raffaele Ingami for the priestly jubilee of Leo XIII, whose name was Gioacchino Pecci; Catholic nations each paid for a chapel, so there are fourteen "national" chapels, and the Tsar gave two columns of the portal. It stands in Prati, the new quarter built after 1870 by the Italian state right next to the Vatican, and it is the papacy's answer in stone.
Look up at the iron frieze under the roof: cypresses, stars and lilies from Leo XIII's coat of arms. During the German occupation, refugees hid inside the dome.

The Waldensians are Italy's oldest Protestant church, persecuted for centuries and allowed to build in Rome only after 1870. In 1911–14 they put up this church on Piazza Cavour, facing the Palace of Justice. Behind the Romanesque-looking stone is a load-bearing frame of reinforced concrete, the first in a Roman church (Emanuele Rutelli and Paolo Bonci; the façade from Pazzi's rival design). The style was chosen to be "national and Protestant": churchy, but deliberately not Catholic. Its bell towers have no bells.

The clue: the lunette over the door, a lit candelabrum in a dark forest with the motto LUX LUCET IN TENEBRIS, "the light shines in the darkness", the Waldensian emblem. Inside, Paolo Paschetto's Liberty stained glass is arranged in three tiers: figures, flowers, geometry.
Practical: opening hours for visitors are short; concerts are a good way in.
tempio-valdese.s: chiesavaldesepiazzacavour.it; Turismo Roma; romasegreta.it; Google Places

p: When the ghetto was demolished after 1870, Rome's Jews, the oldest Jewish community in Europe, built their great synagogue on the cleared land by the river, high enough to be seen across the city. Osvaldo Armanni and Vincenzo Costa designed it in 1901–04 in an eclectic Assyrian-Babylonian style, deliberately unlike any church, under the only square-based dome in Rome, clad in aluminium.

Downstairs, the Spanish-rite oratory (Tempio Spagnolo) was fitted out in 1932 with marbles saved from the Cinque Scole, the five synagogues that shared one building in the ghetto. The museum tells the story from the ghetto to the round-up of 16 October 1943 and the 1982 terrorist attack outside the doors, in which two-year-old Stefano Gaj Taché was killed.
The clue: from the Lungotevere, catch the metallic sheen of the dome; inside, the women's gallery and the Spanish-rite marbles.
Practical: visits only through the museum, with a guide, after a security check. Not on Saturdays.
synagogue.s: Museo Ebraico di Roma; estateromana.com; visitlazio.com; Google Places

sacro-cuore-euclide.t: Sacro Cuore Immacolato di Maria, Piazza Euclide
p: The church looks oddly squat because it is missing its top. Armando Brasini began it in 1923, with money from Italian-Canadians, as a cross inside a circle with four bastion-like chapels, and planned a dome that would have reached 100 m to the cross, higher than the hills around it and a rival to St Peter's across the river. The money ran out; work stopped at the drum in 1951, leaving a base built for a dome 23 m across inside, which would have been the largest in Rome after the Vatican's.

Brasini was a showman of grand classical schemes under Fascism, and the building is a monument to what the 1920s thought Rome should look like. Without its dome, the interior is a huge, low, oddly calm space.
The clue: at the inner corner of the right-hand central pier stands the plaster model of the dome that was never built. Look also for Brasini's models of the four Evangelists meant for the pinnacles.

Marcello Piacentini, later the chief architect of Fascist Rome, designed this church over ten years; it ended up with plain geometric volumes, two bell towers and no ornament, the three rough arches of the façade echoing the Milanese "Novecento" style. Domus counts it among the five key Roman churches of the century. Inside, Achille Funi's frescoes.

Arnaldo Foschini designed it in 1939 for the planned 1942 World's Fair; it was finished only in 1955–58. A Greek cross clad in travertine under a 32 m hemispherical dome, it sits on a rise at the end of Viale Europa, built to be seen from the whole quarter. Dario Argento filmed *Tenebre* nearby.

s-rita-campitelli.t: Santa Rita in Campitelli (Sala Santa Rita)
p: Carlo Fontana's little church of 1643 stood at the foot of the Aracoeli steps. In the late 1920s the Governatorato demolished everything there to "free" the Capitol and the Theatre of Marcellus, and the church was dismantled stone by stone and rebuilt here. The remains of a medieval church, San Biagio de Mercato, were found when it was taken down. It is deconsecrated and used by the city for free exhibitions.

Alberto Tonelli built this round church for the Servite order in 1946–56. Locals say they passed it a thousand times without noticing; it is listed among Rome's brutalist churches on Italian Wikipedia, though it is closer to a stripped classicism. A quick stop between Villa Torlonia and Porta Pia.
sette-fondatori.s: it.wikipedia (category of brutalist churches); Google Places reviews

p: On the Gianicolo, where the defenders of the Roman Republic fought the French in 1849, Giovanni Jacobucci built a half-underground ossuary, inaugurated on 3 November 1941. Thirty-six niches name more than 1,600 dead of 1849–70, including Andrea Aguyar, "Garibaldi's Moor". The clue: Goffredo Mameli's porphyry tomb (he wrote Italy's anthem and died here at 21), and the bronze braziers with wolves' heads at the corners.
ossario-garibaldino.s: Sovrintendenza Capitolina; Ministero della Cultura; Google Places

p: In the housing estates of Casal Bruciato stands a church that looks like an upturned hull. Saverio Busiri Vici built it in 1965–71 entirely in exposed concrete: fat diagonal piers lean out from the walls, and long wall-beams run round the top like a ship's gunwale. The front curves in, the back curves out, and ribbon windows are cut into the concrete. Domus picks it as Rome's example of "structural brutalism", with a nod to Le Corbusier's naval look.

Inside it is bare on purpose: a column of stained glass behind the altar, fixed furnishings, and a floor of concrete and river gravel, so the materials speak for themselves. Turismo Roma notes, a little sadly, that the building still looks unfinished; that is what makes it.

Busiri Vici (1929–2023) came from a dynasty of Roman architects and worked for decades for the Vatican, including the extension of Casa Santa Marta; this church and Villa Ronconi are his best-known works.
The clue: find the floor of river pebbles, and the stained-glass column. Pair it with San Vincenzo Pallotti, 900 m away.
visitazione.s: Domus (Feb 2025); Turismo Roma; Avvenire (Aug 2023); SOS Brutalism

p: Designed by Bevilacqua, Breccia Fratadocchi and Feci, consecrated in 1996, it covers a central plan with a saddle-shaped concrete vault. The clue from BeWeB: a sunken baptismal pool fed by water spilling from a travertine boulder.
pallotti.s: BeWeB (Le Chiese moderne di Roma); Turismo Roma

p: Vivina Rizzi and Ennio Canino designed it in 1957–65 for the Missionaries of La Salette, in Monteverde above the Portuense. The plan is an ellipse with wavy, lobed walls, and the roof is a concrete tent folded into eight segments at alternating heights, so daylight comes in through slots between them in cones. The detached triangular bell tower looks, as one visitor puts it, like an airport control tower.

It was treated as a prototype for the church buildings of the following decades, not only the church itself but the complex around it: auditorium, halls, sports ground. BeWeB counts it among Rome's key modern churches.
The clue: stand under the centre and look up at the alternating roof segments and the light coming between them.

The title was the idea of the first parish priest, Francesco Rauti, and Pius XII and John XXIII liked it: a church to show the Church's presence in the world of work, in the working-class Portuense. Raffaello Fagnoni built a cylinder of red stone with thin travertine bands, and in front of it a cylindrical bell tower that doubles as the entrance portal, joined to the church by a footbridge at first-floor level.

Inside, an oval hall stands on fourteen concrete piers clad in stone, carrying a ribbed ceiling of primary and secondary beams. A gallery runs round at first-floor level under a ribbon window decorated outside with a row of crosses. Domus chose it as the example of a "minor" architecture that surprises by its sobriety.
The clue: the bell tower's top, a lattice of concrete piers through which you can see the bells.

From outside it reads as a pyramid, and some visitors see the Eye of Providence in it. Pier Luigi Nervi designed it with his son Antonio in 1976; Pier Luigi died in 1979 and Antonio finished it in 1981. The square plan is entered from one corner, so you walk in on the diagonal, and the floor slopes down towards the altar; the roof is a pyramid of prefabricated beams springing from diagonal frames and covered in copper. An eye-shaped stained-glass window watches the hall.

Nervi was the great Italian concrete engineer of the century (the Palazzetto dello Sport, the Corso Francia viaduct, the Paul VI audience hall), and here you see his ribs and prefabrication used for a parish church. The drawings are in the MAXXI archive, no. 335. Masonic readings of the eye are folklore.
The clue: Andrea Martini's bronze Stations of the Cross, which run round the walls in one unbroken band. Their fibreglass models are kept at San Frumenzio.
s-gaspare.s: MAXXI Nervi archive; MiC Censimento delle architetture contemporanee; it.wikipedia; Google Places

p: Mario Paniconi and Giulio Pediconi, a partnership that had worked for Fascist EUR, designed this church in the Roma Est estates in 1966–70. A huge roof sits on four piers so that it seems to hover over the hall, and a small cylindrical weekday chapel is capped by a quarter-sphere. Inside it is a big box, "a good place to pray on your own if you appreciate numinous spaces", as the Churches of Rome Wiki author puts it.
Giuseppe Cafasso, the Turin priest the church is named for, was the patron of prisoners condemned to death, a link to the confraternities of San Giovanni Decollato across town.

madre-redentore.t: Santa Maria Madre del Redentore, Tor Bella Monaca
p: In the middle of Tor Bella Monaca, the 1980s estate built for 30,000 people on the city's eastern edge, rises a triangular mass of raw concrete with two pinnacles. Pierluigi Spadolini designed it in 1985–87 and Riccardo Morandi engineered the roof. There is no cross on the top: the sun shining between the two pinnacles makes it, and a long slit window runs from the apse to the entrance.

Inside, Mario Ceroli's wooden crucifix rises, the parish says, almost 15 metres. Visitors praise the raw concrete and its texture and regret the cheerful modern furnishings. Domus notes its "twin", Spadolini's church in Naples.

The estate around it is part of the visit: Barucci's eight-storey "Serpentone" and four towers, a demolish-and-rebuild plan by Léon Krier that never happened, and EU-funded renovation now. The church was meant as the estate's landmark, and it is.
The clue: find where the light makes the cross; and the slit window.
madre-redentore.s: Turismo Roma; parish site smmr.it; Domus (Jan 2026); vediromainbici; Google Places

p: The largest mosque in Italy, opened at the summer solstice of 1995, it was designed by Paolo Portoghesi with Vittorio Gigliotti and Sami Mousawi. Permission came with two conditions: no loudspeaker call to prayer, and a dome lower than St Peter's.

The prayer hall is the reason to come. Each column splits into three stems that branch into the ribs of the vault, so you stand in a grove of concrete palms under a stepped dome ringed by smaller ones. Portoghesi, a historian of Borromini, mixed Islamic geometry with the Roman Baroque, and it shows: this is the most Borrominian building of 20th-century Rome.
The clue: follow one column up until its three stems separate.
Practical: free; Friday is prayer only; groups book ahead; Open House Roma and the Touring Club run free visits.
mosque.s: Open House Roma; Touring Club Italiano; prolocoroma.it; funweek.it; Google Places

p: Three curved white walls rise over an ordinary housing estate like sails, the tallest 26 m high, and the light falls between them into a calm, bright hall. Richard Meier won the Vicariate's competition for the "church of the year 2000"; work began on 1 March 1998 and it opened on 26 October 2003. It was the flagship of "50 churches for Rome 2000", a programme to give new parishes to the outer estates where hundreds of thousands of people lived without a nearby church.

The sails are precast blocks of white cement with titanium dioxide, meant to clean themselves in sunlight by breaking down dirt (photocatalysis): a nice chemistry point to check against how white they look today. Sources disagree on the blocks' weight: Turismo Roma says 256 panels of 12 tonnes, Meier told Architectural Record about 8 tons each.

The three sails stand for the Trinity, and three skylights continue the idea. Visitors note that the building has no air conditioning and can be warm in summer, and a fence that was not in Meier's design now closes the churchyard.
The clue: stand at the back of the nave and watch the light move across the curved inner face of the sails.
jubilee-church.s: Turismo Roma; Architectural Record; parish site; Domus (Jan 2026); Google Places

p: One of the "50 churches for Rome 2000", it is often called the artists' church: Mimmo Paladino made the Stations of the Cross, Carla Accardi a stained-glass window, and other well-known Italian artists contributed works. Sartogo and Grenon built a plain box outside and a light, half-domed space within, with a huge window.

Opinions differ: Siviaggia calls it the most successful mix of religious art and modern architecture in Rome; a local reviewer calls it "more photogenic than beautiful". Decide for yourself, then cross the road to Santa Passera, a medieval church on a Roman tomb, for the strongest then-and-now pairing on the map.

In the new Giardino di Roma district on the south-western edge, Anselmi & Associati built in 2007–10 a church that is all structure: three sinusoidal parabolic arches of different heights and angles, leaning against each other and meeting the ground only at their ends. They are carried on custom-made twisted steel beams, and the roof between them is covered with a mosaic of aquamarine tile shards, broken on site.

The parish was founded on 1 October 2000, a few months after Padre Pio's beatification, and met outdoors or in temporary rooms for years while the neighbourhood was still a building site. Inside, mosaic walls surround a figure of the saint.
The clue: find the points where the arches touch the ground, and look up at how little holds the roof.

In the Prenestino industrial area, among warehouses of Chinese wholesalers, a door in a wall opens on curved roofs, red columns and a hall of golden Buddhas. Hua Yi Si opened on 1 April 2013, paid for by the Chinese community of Rome and donors in China and Taiwan, and modelled on the Chung Tai Chan monastery in Taiwan. Centro Astalli and the FAI both call it the largest Chinese Buddhist temple in Europe.

It is a working monastery, with a Chan (Zen) hall for 150 and monthly meditation in Italian. For the map it is the end point of the same story the mosque and the synagogue tell: Rome's newer faiths building their own landmarks.
hua-yi-si.s: Centro Astalli; FAI; vabbeiovado.com; Google Places

vitinia.t: Sacro Cuore di Gesù Agonizzante, Vitinia
p: Ildo Avetta, an Argentine architect of Piedmontese origin who designed many churches, built this one in 1955. The Churches of Rome Wiki author calls it "one of the best churches in Rome of the period, and deserves to be better known". Listed by Italian Wikipedia among Rome's brutalist churches. Not yet verified by a second architectural source, so judge it on the spot; it is on the way to San Pio at Malafede.
vitinia.s: Google Places reviews (incl. Churches of Rome Wiki author); it.wikipedia; map pin approximate

p: Abruzzini's church in Val Melaina has a stepped interior where the congregation sits in front of and around the altar, under a tent-like roof with strips of glass. It holds the fibreglass models of Andrea Martini's bronze Stations of the Cross made for Nervi's San Gaspare del Bufalo.

Glauco and Roberto Gresleri built it in 1997–2000 on a slope below Via di Torrevecchia, so you go down to enter. The round hall is crossed by a stalactite cross of two interlocking blades that carries the light from the dome down to the altar, and the roof is a hanging garden for parish festivals. Pope Leo XIV visited the parish on 8 March 2026. (A different building by Nemesi, the civic-religious centre at Quartaccio, is often confused with it.)

Milanese architects Monestiroli built this rational, linear church on a raised forecourt for a parish that had spent ten years in a shop. Light comes through white cement blocks and down the tower above the altar. Reviews are split between "very impressive" and "a bit dull"; a stop for those doing the south.
s-carlo-fonte-laurentina.s: Turismo Roma; Archidiap; Google Places reviews

p: Built in 2001–09 by Andrej Obolenskij in the grounds of Villa Abamelek, 29 m high, it was described as the largest Russian Orthodox church built abroad since 1917. It stands within sight of the Apostolic Palace, a statement in a city where the two churches had been estranged since 1054. Go for the view of St Peter's dome from the steps and for the icon given by Patriarch Alexy II.
s-caterina-russian.s: L'Esodo; Turismo Roma; prolocoroma.it; Google Places

p: Italy's first Latter-day Saints temple was dedicated in March 2019 on the northern edge of the city, with olive groves and a cascading fountain. The clue: in the visitor centre, the full-size replica of an Italian farmhouse façade and the hall shaped like a forum. Strange, sincere and very un-Roman.

Francesco Berarducci (the architect of Villino Berarducci) built it in the late 1970s to mid-1980s near the catacombs of St Valentine. Geometric cubes, square floor tiles and a metal roof meant, one reviewer says, to echo Roman ruins; the weekday chapel was given to the Orthodox. Combine with the Villaggio Olimpico and the Corso Francia viaduct.
Designed by Giuseppe Spina and finished in 1991, with mosaics by Rupnik's Centro Aletti (2000). Worth a stop only if you are doing the northern estates with San Frumenzio.

nome-maria.t: Santissimo Nome di Maria in Via Latina
p: Visitors describe "exposed reinforced concrete" and a nativity scene kept up all year. Architect still to be confirmed; on the way between the Appia and the Tuscolano.

corpo-sangue.t: SS. Corpo e Sangue di Cristo
p: A low square hall with load-bearing elements in exposed concrete; even its admirers call it "not very interesting as a building". On the map for completeness of the brutalist list.

suffragio.t: Sacro Cuore del Suffragio and the Purgatory museum
p: Built in 1894–1917 by Giuseppe Gualandi, the church looks lost from Lombardy. In the sacristy corridor is the strangest museum in Rome: a single case of books, cloth and wood with burnt handprints and fingerprints, collected by a French priest, Victor Jouët, as messages from souls asking for prayers. The oldest item claims to date from 1731. Presented by the church as testimony; no scientific examination is on record.
suffragio.s: Churches of Rome Wiki; visitor reports

p: Corviale is one building, nine storeys high and almost a kilometre long, laid across a ridge at the south-western edge of Rome so that the city stops on one side and the Campagna begins on the other. Mario Fiorentino's team designed it in the 1970s on the model of Le Corbusier's Unité d'habitation: a "street" of shops and services was meant to run along the fourth floor, the piano libero.

The services never came. In the 1980s the free floor was occupied by families who walled off flats for themselves, and Corviale became shorthand for failed social housing. It is also the opposite story now: the Lazio Region's "chilometro verde" project is turning the occupied floor into legal flats, and EU recovery money (about €58 million in the PUI 24 programme) has redone the squares, an open-air theatre, the library and two parks, mostly finished by June 2026.
Fiorentino also designed the Fosse Ardeatine memorial, so he made both Rome's most powerful concrete space and its most notorious concrete block.
Practical: the street art at the ends and the view along the slab from Via di Poggio Verde are the classic shots. It is home to some 4,500 people; behave as in anyone's courtyard.
corviale.s: Laboratorio di Città Corviale; Roma Capitale; Regione Lazio

p: Laurentino 38 was Rome's biggest public-housing plan of its time, a car-shaped quarter strung along a ring road. Its signature is a set of "ponti", housing blocks that bridge the road on stilts, designed to carry shops and services over the traffic. There were eleven; three were demolished in 2006, leaving eight.

The bridges became occupied and run-down, and the estate a byword for the failed periphery. ATER's conversion of bridges 5 and 6 into 56 flats has dragged on since 2022, and the L38 Squat social centre on the sixth bridge, there for about 35 years, was cleared by police on 28 April 2026.
Walk or cycle the ring to see the whole sequence; the first bridge, now the Municipio IX office, is the easiest one to stand under.

tuscolano-libera.t: Tuscolano: Libera's "horizontal unit" and the INA-Casa estate
p: Behind a rough tufa wall on Via Selinunte is one of the most original pieces of postwar Italian housing: Adalberto Libera's Unità di abitazione orizzontale, 200 homes for about 1,000 people, mostly single-storey patio houses packed together like a Moroccan medina, plus a gallery block of small flats. You go in through a single vaulted gate.

Around it is Tuscolano, Rome's largest INA-Casa estate (the state's 1949–63 housing plan): 112 buildings and 3,150 flats for about 18,000 people. Saverio Muratori and Mario De Renzi planned Tuscolano II with its long V-shaped block, and the Parco degli Acquedotti, with the arches of the Roman aqueducts, is at the end of the street.
Pasolini filmed *Mamma Roma* (1962) here: the new flats that are meant to lift Anna Magnani's son out of the slums.
tuscolano-libera.s: ASF Lazio; Pandora Rivista; Ecomuseo Via Latina; MiC Atlante architettura contemporanea

p: The borgate were the estates where the regime moved the poor it cleared from the centre. Quarticciolo, by Roberto Nicolini (1939–43), is the last and the most ordered: a grid with a cardo and decumanus (Via Manfredonia and Via Ostuni) like a Roman camp, gallery-access and terraced blocks, and a tower on the square that was the Casa del Fascio and later a police station.

In the occupation it was the turf of Giuseppe Albano, "il Gobbo del Quarticciolo", a teenage partisan and bandit who became a local legend. Today it is a tight-knit, poor quarter with its own social centres.
quarticciolo.s: it.wikipedia; Open House Roma; Lucy sulla cultura

villaggio-olimpico.t: Villaggio Olimpico and the Corso Francia viaduct
p: For the 1960 Olympics, Libera, Moretti, Monaco, Luccichenti and Cafiero built a village for about 8,000 athletes, later rehoused for state employees: low blocks on pilotis with ribbon windows and yellow brick, laid out like a Roman castra. Over it runs Pier Luigi and Antonio Nervi's Corso Francia viaduct, about a kilometre of road on 110-odd concrete piers that open like butterflies. Walk underneath it: it is the best free Nervi in Rome. Next to it, Morandi's Via Olimpica viaduct and Brasini's monumental Ponte Flaminio.
Vigna Clara station nearby was built for the 1990 World Cup and used for eight days, then sat empty for 32 years; it has run again since June 2022.
villaggio-olimpico.s: Comune di Roma; Open House Roma; RFI (2022, 2026)

p: The grandstand canopy is a row of eleven hyperbolic-paraboloid concrete shells on sculptural pillars, said to have been the largest such shell structure in the world. The trotting track opened on 26 December 1959 for the Olympic years and closed on 30 January 2013 to make way for AS Roma's stadium and a Libeskind business park.

The stadium never came: the heritage office protected the grandstand in 2017, Roma dropped the plan in February 2021 and moved to Pietralata, and the site has been rotting since, with squatters drying laundry at the gate and a fire in 2026. In August 2026 the local council voted to make the river bend a nature and sports park.
Do not go in. The structure is unsafe and the stables have asbestos roofs; the shells are best seen from outside, across the field.

Santiago Calatrava's City of Sport was started in 2005 for the 2009 World Swimming Championships, which took place elsewhere. The money ran out with a 75 m, 6,800-tonne steel sail standing in a field, and it stayed that way for more than fifteen years, visible from much of eastern Rome.

In 2021 it passed to the state property agency; €80 million made the halls safe and added parks and roads, and it was handed back to the city on 7 July 2025 for the Youth Jubilee. It now hosts events (a Ferrari show in May 2026, a concert in July). A €981 million research-campus proposal was filed in October 2026, a proposal only.

Built for the 1960 Olympics on the site of the Fascist Stadio Nazionale, the Flaminio was Italy's rugby stadium until 2011 and has been empty since. The Getty's "Keeping It Modern" programme paid for a conservation plan; in February 2026 Lazio football club presented a €480 million plan by Marco Casamonti to build a much bigger stadium over it, opposed by the Nervi family, and a Roman necropolis is reported under the west stand. A conditional yes came in September 2026; nothing has started. See it as Nervi left it while you can.

A 61 m concrete dome assembled from 1,620 prefabricated pieces and held down by flying buttresses that splay out like the legs of a tent; much of it was prefabricated, so the dome rose in 40 days. Recently restored. Five minutes from the Flaminio and the Villaggio Olimpico.
palazzetto.s: Google Places reviews; Open House Roma

p: EUR was laid out for the 1942 Universal Exhibition, cancelled by the war. Its symbol is the Palazzo della Civiltà Italiana: six storeys of arches, nine per row (a play on the letters of "Benito Mussolini", some say), with a slogan about a "people of poets, artists, heroes, saints". Fendi has used it as its headquarters since 2015. It is a tourist icon, so keep it short, and pair it with the Velodromo crater and the Museum of Roman Civilisation (Spectre's funeral).

foro-italico.t: Foro Italico and Stadio dei Marmi
p: Enrico Del Debbio built the Stadio dei Marmi in 1928–32 as part of the Foro Mussolini, now Foro Italico. Sixty 4 m marble athletes, each paid for by an Italian city, stand round the track; at the entrance an obelisk still carries MUSSOLINI DUX, and the propaganda mosaics of the avenue survived the fall of the regime. It is free to walk in.

Built for the 1960 Games with a track of Cameroon hardwood, unused after 1968, the velodrome was imploded on 24 July 2008, spreading asbestos dust over EUR. The housing planned in its place never came; what you see is a grassy crater about 66,000 m² on ground with high flood and landslide risk. A monument to the gap between plans and Rome.

The Roma–Fiuggi railway was a narrow-gauge line opened in 1916 that ran from Termini past Porta Maggiore and along the Casilina into the hills. It was cut back in stages (1982, 2008, 2015) and the last stretch to Centocelle closed on 4 March 2026. Tracks, bridges and the Porta Maggiore crossing are left, already used for tents and dumping. Further out, at Centocelle, are the depot and a 1941 metro tunnel later used as a mushroom farm.

The Forlanini was built under Fascism as a model sanatorium, named after Carlo Forlanini, the doctor who invented the artificial pneumothorax for tuberculosis. It closed in June 2015. The giant kitchen is buried in rubble, film crews rent the colonnades (€14,400 for two weeks in 2026), and in June 2026 the hospital company's director said the closed building cost €700,000 a year in water, more than the working San Camillo next door. A 2024 Italy–Holy See declaration earmarked it for the Bambino Gesù children's hospital.
forlanini.s: it.wikipedia; RomaToday (Feb 2026); Abitare a Roma; Secolo d'Italia (Jun 2026)

s-maria-pieta.t: Santa Maria della Pietà and the Museo della Mente
p: The asylum of Santa Maria della Pietà opened in 1913 on Monte Mario: about 130 hectares and more than thirty pavilions, a city for people the city did not want. It worked until Italy closed its asylums after the Basaglia law of 1978; the last patients left in the late 1990s.

Today it is a public park. Some pavilions are offices, some are still abandoned, and in 2015 twenty-eight street artists painted their façades. The Museo Laboratorio della Mente in Pavilion 6 reopened in 2026: an interactive museum on madness and how it was treated, mostly in Italian but with an English booklet.
s-maria-pieta.s: Il Post (2024); Canale Dieci (May 2026); Google Places

p: The Leo Penicillina factory opened on 21 September 1950 in front of Alexander Fleming himself, the first in Italy to make the antibiotic and once one of the biggest in Europe. Production ended in 2006. The 40,000-odd m² of sheds and towers (sources give up to 120,000) became a refuge for hundreds of homeless people and a dump of chemicals and asbestos, with fires and repeated evictions.

It was sold at auction to a Roman property company in 2025; clean-up has started, and demolition, flats and a "memory space" are planned. For a biotechnologist it is the most fitting ruin in Rome. Do not go in: an 18-year-old was badly hurt photographing inside.

Mira Lanza made soap and chemicals here from 1899 to 1957; three listed buildings, including the pyrite furnaces, survive by the river next to Teatro India. Fires and squatting followed, and the French street artist Seth painted the walls. In April 2026 the city approved a free 30-year concession to Roma Tre university for about 300 student beds, so see the ruin now.
mira-lanza.s: Roma Capitale; Radio Colonna; FAI; Google Places

p: The Gazometro was built in 1935 by Ansaldo and Klönne of Dortmund and went into service in 1937 as the largest gasholder in Europe: almost 90 m tall and 63 m across. Around it are the old gasworks, the ex General Markets and, a short walk away, the Centrale Montemartini, a power station whose diesel engines now stand among Roman statues. The best view is from the Ponte della Scienza or from across the river.

ex-snia.t: Ex SNIA Viscosa and Lago Bullicante
p: SNIA Viscosa made artificial silk here until 1954. In 1992 excavations for a shopping centre broke into the water table and the pit filled: the "boiling lake" that residents then defended against developers until the city made it a park. A great chemistry-and-hydrology stop: viscose, acid baths, and an accidental spring.

After 1870 Italy ringed its new capital with 15 forts against a French return of the pope; they were obsolete by 1919. Forte Prenestino, with moat, ramps and Savoy crests, has been occupied since 1986 and is the only one regularly open, through its social centre's events. Walk the tunnels and ramparts; enjoy, and watch your drink at big concerts.

Mussolini lived at Villa Torlonia from 1925 to 1943. Under the house is a cellar converted into an air-raid shelter, and 6 m under the forecourt an armoured bunker begun in December 1942 and unfinished when he was arrested on 25 July 1943. The tour adds a bombing simulation. Visitors find the English guiding thin; read up first.
villa-torlonia-bunker.s: Google Places reviews; Sovrintendenza Capitolina; map pin approximate

p: On 24 March 1944, the day after the partisan bomb in Via Rasella killed 33 German police, the SS took 335 men, prisoners, Jews and passers-by, to these pozzolana quarries and shot them in groups of five, then blew up the entrances. The order was ten Italians for every German, and they killed five more than that.

The memorial of 1949, by a team that included Mario Fiorentino (later the architect of Corviale) and Giuseppe Perugini, leaves the caves as they are and then presses an enormous single concrete slab low over the rows of tombs, lit only from a gap at the edges. You walk in bent, among identical graves.
Practical: free; ANFIM runs free guided visits booked a week ahead. Pair with Via Rasella and Via Tasso for the whole story.
fosse-ardeatine.s: Ministero della Difesa; ANFIM; Google Places

p: For three centuries this was where Rome buried those who could not be buried in Catholic ground: Protestants, Orthodox, Jews, atheists. Keats lies in the old part with the line he chose, "Here lies One Whose Name was writ in Water"; Shelley's ashes lie by the Aurelian wall; Antonio Gramsci, the Communist thinker who died in Fascist custody, is here, and so is Goethe's son August. Henry James buried his Daisy Miller "in an angle of the wall". Cats sleep on the graves.
acattolico.s: Google Places; Henry James, Daisy Miller

verano.t: Verano and the bombing of San Lorenzo
p: The Verano is Rome's monumental cemetery, 83 hectares of tombs and statues, more an open-air museum than a graveyard. On 19 July 1943 Allied bombers aiming at the San Lorenzo rail yards killed some 1,500 people or more in the quarter (estimates vary); the damage in the Quadriportico and the Pincetto Vecchio sections was deliberately left as it was. The raid helped bring down Mussolini six days later. Morante set the bombing at the heart of *La Storia*.

A long concrete complex in the old Castro Pretorio barracks, with reading rooms that researchers praise and security that visitors find "like a prison". Worth a look from outside on the way to San Lorenzo.
bnc.s: Italian Art Journal; Google Places reviews

p: The big sister of the Palazzetto: a 100 m prestressed-concrete dome on the EUR lake, built for the 1960 Games and now a concert hall under a sponsor's name.

Elena Luzzatto designed it in the 1930s (consecrated 1941). Semicircular niche blocks, a Roman villa inside the grounds, a monument to Yugoslav partisans (1978), Catholic, Jewish, Islamic and Polish sections, and a "Garden of Memories" where ashes are scattered from a basin. Also a mess: the ossuary floods and cladding slabs fell in April 2026.

Walk up Via Rasella from Via del Tritone and look at the walls of no. 139 and the corner of Via del Boccaccio: round, ragged holes 5–15 cm across, about a hundred of them. On 23 March 1944 partisans of the GAP hid a bomb in a rubbish cart outside Palazzo Tittoni as a column of German police marched past, killing 33 of them; the survivors fired wildly at the windows. When the façade was repainted, the holes were deliberately left.

It was the largest partisan attack on German troops in occupied Italy, and its answer came the next day at the Fosse Ardeatine, where 335 men were shot. Whether the attack was justified has been argued in Italy ever since, in courts and newspapers; that is why there is still no plaque in the street.
Look also above no. 17 opposite, where a few shrapnel marks remain.

In 1943–44 the SS security police used this apartment block as offices and prison. Resistance fighters, Jews and suspects were held and tortured here; many were taken to the Fosse Ardeatine or to La Storta to be shot. The cells keep the messages scratched by prisoners, including calendars and farewells. The museum was itself bombed by neo-fascists in the 1990s. English captions are thin.
via-tasso.s: Google Places; Museo Storico della Liberazione

p: Four temples of the Republic lie below the modern street, dug out in the 1920s when a whole quarter was demolished. Behind them stood the Curia of Pompey, where the Senate met on the Ides of March 44 BC and Caesar was stabbed: a banner marks the spot. The cats of the sanctuary are what most people photograph.

Bruno taught that the universe was infinite and full of worlds, and refused to recant. He was burned alive here, gagged, on 17 February 1600. The bronze by Ettore Ferrari went up in 1889, paid for by anticlerical and Masonic groups as a deliberate provocation facing the Vatican, and it still faces it. Come early, when the market is just setting up.

moro.t: Via Caetani: where Aldo Moro was found
p: On 16 March 1978 the Red Brigades ambushed Aldo Moro, leader of the Christian Democrats, in Via Fani in the north of the city, killing his five bodyguards. After 55 days they shot him and left the car here, in a narrow street placed almost exactly between the headquarters of the Christian Democrats and the Communist Party, the two parties Moro had been bringing together. A bronze relief and plaque mark the spot. The Via Fani ambush site has its own memorial.

After a short bombardment the Bersaglieri entered through a breach next to Michelangelo's gate, and Rome became Italy's capital. A column marks the breach; the Bersaglieri museum is in the gate. The British Embassy by Basil Spence (1971), across the street, was designed to answer Michelangelo's gate in concrete clad in travertine.

ghetto.t: The Ghetto and the round-up of 16 October 1943
p: At dawn on 16 October 1943 the SS sealed the old ghetto and took 1,259 people; 1,023 were deported to Auschwitz and 16 came back. Stolpersteine, small brass stones set in the pavement by Gunter Demnig, name them house by house along Via del Portico d'Ottavia, and Largo 16 Ottobre 1943 is named for the day. The ghetto itself, walled from 1555 to 1870, was demolished after unification; the Great Synagogue stands on its edge.

Matteotti had denounced the violence and fraud of the 1924 election in parliament. On 10 June, walking to the tram, he was pushed into a car here; a neighbour heard the horn blaring to cover his screams. His body was found in August in the Quartarella woods near Riano. Jorio Vivarelli's 1974 bronze, "The idea, death", quotes him: "Kill me, but you will never kill the idea in me."

gullace.t: Teresa Gullace plaque, Viale Giulio Cesare
p: Teresa Gullace came to the barracks of the 81st Infantry, where her husband was held after a round-up, and was shot when she pushed through to speak to him. The same afternoon partisans attacked the barracks in her name; the UDI women's union put up the plaque in October 1945. Rossellini turned her into Anna Magnani's Pina, but filmed the scene in Via Montecuccoli (see that stop).

The plaque says she was "killed by the violence of the regime"; feminists put it up without permission, the Interior Minister wanted it removed, and the city kept it. In 2025 the anniversary flowers were stolen. It is the clearest marker in central Rome of the "Years of Lead".

The bridge was built in England and assembled here in 1862–63 for the railway to Civitavecchia. The plaque names ten women said to have been shot against the railing on 7 April 1944 after raiding a bakery. In 2023 Giorgio Guidoni's book concluded that none of them died here that day, and the national Atlas of Nazi-Fascist massacres removed the episode. Read the plaque as a case study in how memory is built.
ponte-industria.s: straginazifasciste.it; it.wikipedia; ANSA; map pin approximate

cannon-montorio.t: San Pietro in Montorio: the 1849 cannonball
p: In 1849 Garibaldi's volunteers defended the short-lived Roman Republic on the Gianicolo against the French army sent to restore the pope. The ball lodged in the left flank of San Pietro in Montorio has a plaque recalling June 1849. Three more are on the map: on the altar wall of San Bartolomeo all'Isola, on the stairs of the Galleria Colonna, and (perhaps replicas) in the gate of Villa Pamphilj.

cannon-colonna.t: Galleria Colonna: the cannonball on the stairs
p: The Colonna kept the ball where it fell, on the steps down into the Sala Grande, one of the most lavish Baroque rooms in Rome. Whether it was aimed at the Quirinal or at the Colonna is unclear (legend). The Sala Grande is also where Audrey Hepburn's princess holds the press conference at the end of *Roman Holiday*.

flood-1277.t: Arco dei Banchi: the 1277 flood plaque
p: Under the painted vault of the Arco dei Banchi, next to a Madonna, is a Latin plaque recording the Tiber flood of November 1277; a line marks how high the water rose. Rome has more than 100 such flood plaques, the city's own hydrological record. The worst flood, Christmas 1598, reached 19.56 m on the Ripetta gauge and is recorded on twelve of them. The river was only tamed by the embankment walls built after the flood of 1870.
flood-1277.s: it.wikipedia (Piene del Tevere a Roma); Comune di Roma; ISPRA

flood-minerva.t: Santa Maria sopra Minerva: the flood ladder
p: The plaques on the right of the façade include 1422 (said to be the oldest still at its true water level), 1495 and 1870, each with a hand or line pointing to where the water stood. Inside is Rome's only Gothic church, built over a temple, and in the adjoining Dominican convent Galileo knelt and abjured on 22 June 1633. Bernini's elephant carries the obelisk outside.
flood-minerva.s: Comune di Roma; ISPRA; Google Places

p: The Porto di Ripetta was a Baroque river port of 1704 with curving steps down to the water, destroyed by the embankments of the 1880s. What survives are two columns in a little garden with the great floods marked on them, and the Ripetta hydrometer set in the side of San Rocco. Its zero is still Rome's reference: ordinary flood alert at 10 m, "extraordinary" above 13 m, the record 19.56 m in 1598, 17.22 m in 1870, and the last overtopping 16.84 m in December 1937.

The Cloaca Maxima began as a drain for the marshy Forum valley and became Rome's main sewer. Its outlet into the Tiber, an arch of peperino stone in three rings dated about 120–80 BC, was left visible when the 19th-century walls were built. Look for it on the left bank just downstream of the broken Ponte Rotto.

The slightly acidic, fizzy water ("acetosa") was prized for cures; Paul V built a first fountain in 1613 and Alexander VII the exedra in 1661. Goethe is said to have walked out to drink it during his Roman stay. The spring was closed in 1959–66 (sources differ) for groundwater pollution and the fountain now runs on mains water. A chemistry stop on the way to the Mosque.

Augustus brought the obelisk of Psammetichus II from Egypt and set it up as the gnomon of a huge sun-dial on the Campus Martius. A fragment of the real Augustan meridian line, with Greek zodiac labels, lies about 5 m below a building at Via di Campo Marzio 48 (occasional visits). The 1998 line in the piazza is decorative and does not work as a meridian.

angeli-meridian.t: Santa Maria degli Angeli: the 1702 meridian
p: Francesco Bianchini laid the line for Clement XI; at solar noon a beam through a hole in the wall falls on it, and the zodiac signs show the season. It was used to test the Gregorian calendar. The church itself, carved by Michelangelo out of the bath halls, is the grandest example on the map of an ancient building turned into a church.

collegio-romano.t: Collegio Romano and the Calandrelli tower
p: The Torre Calandrelli (1787) rises at the south-east corner of the Collegio Romano. In 1852 the Jesuit astronomer Angelo Secchi, a pioneer of stellar spectroscopy, moved his observatory onto the piers built for Sant'Ignazio's never-built dome. From the 1880s it was Italy's central meteorological office, and in 1888–95 an experimental seismic station. Only the socket of the midday time-ball (1847) remains on the back of Sant'Ignazio's pediment.

panisperna.t: Via Panisperna: the "boys" who started the nuclear age
p: In 1934 Enrico Fermi's group (D'Agostino, Amaldi, Majorana, Rasetti, Pontecorvo, Segrè) found that neutrons slowed down by paraffin and water made elements far more radioactive, the step towards fission. A goldfish fountain in the garden is said to have been the water they used. The building is now inside the Interior Ministry compound; the plaque at the old side entrance is on Via Panisperna (sources disagree on no. 89 or 90, and one visitor reports a plaque on the wrong block).
panisperna.s: Rerum Romanarum; il Bo Live (Univ. Padova); Google Places reviews; map pin approximate

margutta.t: Via Margutta: the rubbish edict and Roman Holiday
p: Rome still has about 67 "mondezzaro" plaques of 1646–1790 forbidding rubbish heaps; this one, from the 1740s, promises fines of ten scudi plus "nerbate, ceppi, giri di rota", lashes, stocks and the wheel, "according to age and sex". Its neighbour in Via del Seminario forbids people, by an accidental double negative, *not* to dump rubbish. At no. 51 is the courtyard of Joe Bradley's flat in *Roman Holiday*; Fellini lived at no. 110.

Mastro Titta's notebook lists 516 names, 514 counted as his executions. He sold painted umbrellas when he was not working, and lived across the river from the city because, by custom, "boia nun passa ponte": the executioner crossed Ponte Sant'Angelo only to work. His cloak and tools are in the Criminology Museum on Via del Gonfalone (check opening).
mastro-titta.s: it.wikipedia (Mastro Titta; Casa del boia); romasegreta.it

p: Found in 1501 and set up by Cardinal Carafa, the statue became the city's notice board for "pasquinades". The best-known, against the Barberini pope who stripped bronze from the Pantheon: "What the barbarians did not do, the Barberini did." Notes are still taped to it.

landsknecht.t: Villa Farnesina: the Landsknecht graffito of 1528
p: The villa of the banker Agostino Chigi is famous for Raphael's frescoes. In the Sala delle Prospettive, among the painted columns, a German soldier of the imperial army that sacked Rome in 1527 scratched a line in Gothic script dated 1528, mocking Clement VII (who had in fact shut himself in Castel Sant'Angelo). It was found during restoration. Similar scratches, one praising Luther, are on Raphael's frescoes in the Vatican.

Pier Paolo Pasolini was a regular at Pommidoro, a family trattoria in working-class San Lorenzo, and Maria Callas came here too. On the evening of 1 November 1975 he dined here with the actor Ninetto Davoli and paid by cheque; hours later he was murdered on the beach at Ostia. The family never cashed the cheque, and it hangs framed inside.

The place closed after the 2020 lockdown, and the owner Aldo Bravi died in 2021; his grandson reopened it in 2023. Reviews praise the carbonara and the tripe. After dinner Pasolini picked up Pino Pelosi at Termini and took him to Al Biondo Tevere on the Ostiense (see that stop).

The late stop on 1–2 November 1975, a few hours before the killing at Ostia; a chair said to be Pasolini's is kept by the entrance. Visconti shot *Bellissima* (1951) here with Anna Magnani. The terrace over the Tiber is the reason locals come.

Pasolini made Pigneto his set for *Accattone*, and Necci was the crew's bar. Myth flag: the owner says the bar seen in the film was a set built in a wine shop at no. 50, with furniture borrowed from Necci. Pigneto is still the neighbourhood of the films: Via Montecuccoli, where *Roma città aperta* was shot, is ten minutes away.

Open since 1922, Rosati was the postwar meeting place of writers and painters; Fellini's café, Canova, is across the square. With Caffè Greco closed since October 2025 and Aragno turned into an Apple Store, it is the best surviving literary café in Rome, if you can take the prices and a 19% service charge.

Founded by the Augustinians and open to all from 1604, the Angelica keeps some 200,000 items in a hall redesigned by Luigi Vanvitelli in the 18th century. No single famous reader is documented, only centuries of scholars. It is also the "Vatican archive" of the *Angels & Demons* film, since the Vatican refused to allow filming.

Wood panelling, blown-glass bookcases and showcases on a sliding rail: the shop looks as it did two centuries ago, and sells rare books, prints and antiques. In *John Wick: Chapter 2* Keanu Reeves comes here for the plans of the catacombs. Buy something small and the owner will tell you the story.

Rossellini shot *Roma città aperta* in 1944–45 with the war barely over, on real streets. Pina, played by Anna Magnani, runs from this doorway after the truck taking her fiancé and is shot down in the street: one of the most famous scenes in cinema. The bombed building she points at, opposite at no. 36, is real.
The scene was based on the death of Teresa Gullace, shot on Viale Giulio Cesare on 3 March 1944 (see that stop). Pigneto and Necci are a few minutes' walk away.
montecuccoli.s: davinotti.com; it.wikipedia; Ecomuseo Casilino; Il Messaggero

crispi-theft.t: Via Francesco Crispi: Ladri di biciclette
p: davinotti.com pins the theft to the columns of no. 18 (now the Gagosian gallery) and the stairs of the old modern-art gallery in the reverse shot. Other scenes: the labour office queue at Via del Gran Paradiso and Via Scarpanto in Val Melaina (with a plaque), and Porta Portese, where a young Sergio Leone appears as a seminarian in the rain.

Fellini shot the fountain scene on winter nights in 1959. Most of the Via Veneto nightlife was rebuilt at Cinecittà (Teatro 5), and the St Peter's dome staircase too; only Ekberg's dawn return at the Excelsior was shot on the real street. Turn round to Santi Vincenzo e Anastasio, the church of the 22 popes' hearts.

The marble mask, probably an ancient drain cover, is said to bite the hands of liars (legend). In *Roman Holiday* (1953) Peck pretends it has; Hepburn's scream was real, the story goes, because she had not been told. The church behind it, Santa Maria in Cosmedin, has an 8th-century crypt cut into Roman remains.

The stairs pass under the old Borgia palace; local tradition calls the lane the Vicus Sceleratus, where Tullia drove her chariot over her father's body (legend). Michelangelo's Moses is at the top. *John Wick: Chapter 2* staged its stair fight here.

mi7-funari.t: Via dei Funari: the yellow Fiat of Mission: Impossible
p: The chase then runs past the Fori Imperiali and down the Spanish Steps; the steps' close-ups were shot on a UK replica and the car was an electric conversion. The "police station" with a real Colosseum view is the former school in Via delle Carine.

continental.t: Rear of the Vittoriano: the Continental (John Wick 2)
p: Interiors are the Grand Hotel Plaza on Via del Corso; Rome's modern-art gallery plays a New York museum, with the Empire State Building added digitally; the party is at the Baths of Caracalla.

gnam-wick.t: Galleria Nazionale d'Arte Moderna: Rome playing New York
p: The skyline behind it was added in post-production. The gallery is worth the visit for itself: a Belle Époque palace of 1911 with Italian art from the 19th and 20th centuries.

spectre-civilta.t: Museum of Roman Civilisation: Spectre's funeral
p: For *Spectre* (2015) the production wanted the Verano; the confraternity that runs it refused, so fake tombs were set between the columns here. The colonnade is pure EUR, built for the cancelled 1942 fair.

ripley-coins.t: San Luigi dei Francesi: Ripley's coin lights
p: The Contarelli chapel holds Caravaggio's St Matthew cycle; the coin-operated lights are real, and *Ripley* (2024) uses them for a scene. Sant'Ivo and the Pantheon are a few steps away.

ad-popolo.t: Santa Maria del Popolo: Angels & Demons
p: The novel's Path of Illumination runs from here to St Peter's Square (the West Ponente relief at the obelisk), Santa Maria della Vittoria (Bernini's Ecstasy of St Teresa), the Four Rivers fountain in Piazza Navona and Castel Sant'Angelo. The Rome diocese refused the film crew, so the church interiors were rebuilt in Hollywood and St Peter's Square was a replica at a racetrack in Inglewood, California. The exteriors are real. The church itself has two Caravaggios in the Cerasi chapel.

The legend: a pet monkey carried a baby to the top of the tower, the father vowed a lamp to the Virgin if the child came down safe, and the lamp has burned ever since (legend). Hawthorne made it the home of his heroine Hilda in *The Marble Faun* (1860). Assassin's Creed Brotherhood also models the nearby Sant'Antonio dei Portoghesi.
hilda-tower.s: Turismo Roma; Hawthorne, The Marble Faun (ch. VI)

p: Goethe came to Rome under a false name and stayed with Tischbein, who painted him lounging in the Campagna. The museum keeps drawings and letters. Myth flag: the story that he was a regular at Caffè Greco does not come from his book.
Carlo Emilio Gadda's "palazzo degli ori" is probably invented, but the city put a plaque at no. 219. The novel's other places, Marino and Pavona in the Castelli, are real; Tor di Gheppio is not.

Painted in 2014 and restored in 2023 with photocatalytic paints, the mammoth nods to the tusks found at Casal de' Pazzi nearby. The slogan reads "Qui ci manca tutto, non ci serve niente": we lack everything, we need nothing.

de-pedis.t: Via del Pellegrino: the end of the Magliana gang's boss
p: The gang ran drugs and gambling in 1970s–80s Rome and was tied to every dark story of the period. De Pedis was then buried, scandalously, in the basilica of Sant'Apollinare until 2012; the link with the disappearance of Emanuela Orlandi is speculation. The gang's base was a bar on Via Chiabrera in Marconi.

Mussolini began digging into Monte Soratte in 1937. From September 1943 to June 1944 it was the headquarters of Field Marshal Kesselring, and Allied bombers hit it in May 1944. From 1967 NATO and the Italian government rebuilt part of it as an anti-atomic shelter for the President and the state's leaders. Just over 4 km of tunnels were dug of a planned 14 km, including a 1.3 km atomic core; the "over 40 km" in some sites has no source.
Since November 2024 an electric narrow-gauge train runs through 2.5 km of galleries that had been closed. Command rooms, dormitories and a power plant survive.

Benedict lived here as a hermit around 500 before founding his order. The monastery clings to the rock in layers of chapels painted from the 13th century on. The clue: Francis of Assisi shown without halo or stigmata, so painted before his canonisation in 1228, probably on a visit in his lifetime.

Monks from Calabria founded it in 1004 and it has kept the Greek rite for a thousand years, inside a Renaissance fortress wall. The clue: in Domenichino's chapel of the founders (1608–10), the young man holding the horse is said to be the painter himself, with Guido Reni and Guercino among the bystanders (tradition).

Sabaudia was founded in 1933–34 on land drained from the Pontine marshes, a showpiece of rationalist planning. Ferruccio Ferrazzi's 15 m mosaic in a parabolic niche shows the Annunciation over a landscape of reclamation; look for the tiny Mussolini at the threshing machine. Today the farms of the plain are worked largely by Punjabi Sikhs, whose gurdwara is in the same town.

Opened on 6 May 1960, it is the burial ground of the German dead of Anzio and the battles for Rome. In *Il sorpasso* (1962) Gassman and Trintignant pass it on their drive. The Commonwealth cemeteries at Anzio are 20 km further on.

Around twenty seats side by side over a channel of running water, with a gutter in front for the sponge on a stick: the latrine by the Forum Baths is the best-preserved public toilet of the Roman world, and the closest match on this map to an ancient urinal still in use.

routes.summary: From the Forum's painted church and the hall-turned-church of Santi Cosma e Damiano to the Capitol, the temples under San Nicola, the Cloaca's mouth, the Tiber island and the Ghetto, ending where Moro's body was found.

routes.summary: Caesar's murder site, Bruno's pyre, the bone crypt of Via Giulia, Pasquino, Borromini's spiral, Pozzo's fake dome, the Jesuit observatory, Augustus' sundial pointer and the flood ladder on the Minerva.

routes.when: Villa Torlonia bunker visits are guided and booked (060608).

routes.when: Villa Farnesina Mon–Sat mornings; the Ossario Garibaldino on Thursday mornings; the Russian church at weekends.
routes.summary: The Landsknecht graffito, two churches with whole basilicas underneath, Giorgiana Masi's plaque, the 1849 cannonball and Bramante's Tempietto, the Garibaldini's crypt and the Russian domes facing St Peter's.

routes.name: Celio and Esquilino: the layered churches
routes.when: Santo Stefano Rotondo is closed Monday; San Clemente's underground is ticketed.
routes.summary: San Clemente's three levels, the fortified Quattro Coronati, the rotunda of martyrs, the Roman houses under Santi Giovanni e Paolo and the SS prison of Via Tasso.

routes.name: Testaccio, Ostiense and Portuense
routes.when: Long distances: tram, bus or bike between the clusters. Santa Passera opens only on Sunday morning.
