routes.when: The Visitazione opens 7:30–12 and 16:30–19; the Penicillina is exterior only.
routes.summary: The bombed Verano, Pasolini's last dinner, the dead railway, Pigneto's bar and the street of Roma città aperta, the accidental lake, then out to Busiri Vici's raw-concrete church, its hyperbolic neighbour, the penicillin ruin and the Rebibbia mammoth.

routes.name: East: Casilina to Tor Bella Monaca
routes.when: Metro and buses; San Gaspare, the Jubilee Church and Hua Yi Si stay open at midday.
routes.summary: Helena's mausoleum and catacomb, two concrete churches, Libera's walled estate, Nervi's San Gaspare, the squatted fort, the last Fascist borgata, Meier's sails, the hidden pagoda, Spadolini's sunlight cross and Calatrava's sail.

routes.name: Appia and EUR
routes.when: Catacombs close at midday; EUR is best by metro B.
routes.summary: Catacombs on the Appia, the Fosse Ardeatine, then EUR: the Square Colosseum, Spectre's fake cemetery, the domed church, the velodrome crater, Laurentino's bridges and Lafuente's rotting grandstand.

routes.name: Far south: Fonte Laurentina to Malafede
routes.when: A car or the Roma–Lido train (Vitinia).
routes.summary: Three late churches on the southern edge: Monestiroli's box, Avetta's 1955 church at Vitinia and Anselmi's tilted arches at Malafede.

routes.name: North edge: Monte Mario to Settebagni
routes.when: A car day; the Museo della Mente and the temple visitor centre are Tue–Sat.
routes.summary: The asylum park and its museum, the Gresleri cylinder, the cemetery city of Prima Porta, two northern concrete churches and the Latter-day Saints temple.

tours.name: Church day: modern religious buildings
tours.intro: Rome's most daring religious buildings since 1890, from an aluminium dome to Meier's sails, with a mosque and a Buddhist temple. The main church day.
tours.how: Metro, train and bus; 7–9 stops. Best on Wednesday or Saturday (Mosque). Catholic churches close about 12–16, so the midday stops are the ones open all day: San Gaspare, the Jubilee Church, Hua Yi Si.
story: After 1870 the new Italian state and the papacy competed in stone: the Church answered the Protestant and Jewish buildings that were suddenly allowed inside the walls, and later raced to put parishes into the housing estates spreading over the Campagna. That race produced Rome's best concrete churches: Busiri Vici, Nervi, Spadolini, and finally Meier for the Jubilee of 2000.
The tour runs in the order of the city, not the calendar: Prati and Parioli in the morning, the eastern estates in the afternoon. Each stop has one thing to find.

stops.note: 1911–14: the first reinforced-concrete church in Rome, built by Protestants. Find the candelabrum lunette.
1897: the aluminium dome with crystal stars.
1920–34: Piacentini's halfway modern.
1923–51: the 100 m dome that never was; its model stands in a pier.
1984–95: columns that branch like palms (Wed/Sat mornings).
1976–81: Nervi's last church, entered at a corner. Open all day.
1998–2003: Meier's sails, self-cleaning white cement. Open all day.
2013: a pagoda behind warehouse walls. Open 10:30–15.
1985–87: the cross made of sunlight between two pinnacles.
1965–71: the rawest concrete church in Rome (from 16:30).
1989–93: a hyperbolic-paraboloid vault, 900 m from the Visitazione.

tours.name: Church hunt through the ages: one day, 1,500 years
tours.intro: The strangest church of each era, oldest first, in one long day: a Byzantine-painted hall, temples under a church, a cannonball, a drilled column, Borromini, Pozzo, a synagogue, Nervi and Meier.
tours.how: Mon, Tue, Thu or Fri only (Sant'Ivo is weekday mornings, San Nicola shuts Wednesday, the Synagogue Saturday). Start 9:30 at the Forum; Sant'Ivo before 13:30; metro east after the Synagogue.
story: Rome is the one city where you can walk the whole history of church building in a day, because almost nothing was ever thrown away: temples became churches, churches were buried under churches, and every age added its own experiment.

stops.note: 6th–9th c.: painted layer on layer, buried by an earthquake.
A medieval church eating three Republican temples.
998: Asclepius' island, and a cannonball of 1849.
Medieval: the drilled column that was probably not a sundial.
1642–60: Borromini's star and spiral.
1685: Pozzo's painted dome.
1901–04: the square aluminium dome.
1976–81: Nervi's pyramid.
2003: Meier's sails.

tours.name: Modern churches of the south-west
tours.intro: A second modern day: tent roofs and ovals of the 1950s–60s, a then-and-now pair in Magliana, the EUR basilica and the tilted arches of Malafede.
tours.how: Bus and tram, then the Roma–Lido train to Vitinia; a car makes it easy.
story: These are the churches of the southern and western estates, from Fagnoni's 'church of work' to the arches of a parish founded the year Padre Pio was beatified.

stops.note: 1957–65: the tent roof that breaks light into cones.
1955–60: the bell tower is the front door.
2006: the artists' church…
…and, across the road, a medieval church on a Roman tomb.
1939–58: the dome that closes EUR.
1955: Avetta's church, said to be one of the best of its time.
2007–10: three arches that touch the ground only at their ends.

tours.name: Under the churches
tours.intro: Go down: houses, temples, tombs and whole basilicas under today's churches, and two catacombs.
tours.how: Most need a small ticket; catacombs are guided and close at midday.
story: In Rome the ground rose by metres over the centuries, and builders reused what was below. These are the places where you can stand inside the earlier city.

stops.note: Three levels down to a Mithraeum.
A shrine painted into a Roman stairwell.
Alleys between temple podiums.
A whole basilica under the trams.
Roman basins: tannery or dye works?
Frescoed galleries and an empress's tomb.
A three-storey stack to a Roman tomb.
A basilica sunk into the catacomb.
Pilgrims' scratched prayers to Peter and Paul.

tours.name: Bones, executioners and the condemned
tours.intro: Rome's relationship with death: the brotherhood that buried the drowned, the friars' bone chapels, the pyre of Bruno, the executioner's house, the baby hatch and the Purgatory museum.
tours.how: Central and walkable; Orazione e Morte may be closed for restoration.
story: The papal city made death public: executions on squares and bridges, confraternities to comfort the condemned and bury the unclaimed, crypts arranged as sermons in bone.

stops.note: Skulls labelled with the cause of death.
3,700 friars arranged as decoration.
Giordano Bruno burned, 1600.
Over 500 executions, and umbrellas.
The wheel for abandoned babies.
Scorch marks said to come from Purgatory.
335 men shot in 1944.

tours.name: The Tiber's record: floods, gauges and the great sewer
tours.intro: Rome wrote down its floods on its walls. Follow the plaques from 1277 to the gauge that still measures the river, and the sewer that has drained it for 2,100 years.
story: Until the embankment walls of the 1880s, the Tiber regularly filled the city: 19.56 m on the Ripetta gauge in 1598. Rome has more than a hundred flood plaques; this is a hydrologist's walk.

stops.note: The oldest flood mark still in the street.
The 1598 mark under the hospital portico.
The gauge that is still Rome's zero.
A ladder of floods, 1422–1870.
The sewer's 2,100-year-old mouth.
The island's well over the sacred spring.

tours.name: Science in the street
tours.intro: Sundials, meridians, an observatory on a church's piers, the lab that opened the nuclear age, a penicillin factory and an accidental lake.
tours.how: Centre on foot, then the outer stops by public transport.
story: Rome was a city of astronomers and calendar-makers long before it was a city of physicists. The trail ends with the chemistry of the 20th century: viscose, antibiotics, and what they left behind.

stops.note: Augustus' sundial pointer.
The 1702 meridian that checked the calendar.
A sighting hole, perhaps.
Secchi's observatory and the time-ball.
Fermi's slow neutrons, 1934.
A mineral spring closed for pollution.
A rayon factory and an accidental lake.
Italy's first penicillin plant, opened by Fleming.

tours.name: 1849: the cannonballs of the Roman Republic
tours.intro: The Roman Republic lasted five months. The French guns that ended it left balls in walls and on altars, and the dead got a Fascist-era crypt.
story: In 1849 Garibaldi and Mazzini defended a republic in Rome against the French army sent to restore Pius IX. The siege of June left its marks across the city.

stops.note: A ball in the church wall.
A ball that stopped on the altar.
A ball left on the palace stairs.
The dead, with Mameli's tomb.

tours.name: Occupied Rome, 1943–44
tours.intro: Nine months of German occupation: the bombs on San Lorenzo, the round-up of the Ghetto, the partisan bomb and its reprisal, the SS prison and the women shot at barracks and bakeries.
tours.how: Centre on foot; Verano, Pigneto and the Fosse Ardeatine by public transport.
story: Rome was bombed in July 1943, occupied in September and liberated on 4 June 1944. The places are small, mostly plaques and marks, but they are exact.

stops.note: The bombing of 19 July 1943.
The round-up of 16 October 1943.
The GAP bomb of 23 March 1944, and the bullet holes.
The reprisal, the next day.
The SS prison.
A mother shot outside a barracks.
Rossellini's version of her death.
A massacre now doubted by historians.

tours.name: Political murder: Matteotti to the Magliana gang
tours.intro: The exact spots of the killings that shaped modern Italy: Matteotti in 1924, Moro in 1978, a student on a bridge in 1977, a gang boss in 1990.
tours.how: All central, on foot or by tram.
story: Each marker records a turning point: the murder that made Mussolini a dictator, the kidnapping that ended the historic compromise, the 'Years of Lead' and the criminal Rome that grew in their shadow.

stops.note: Seized here on 10 June 1924.
Found here on 9 May 1978.
Shot here on 12 May 1977; no one convicted.
Shot here on 2 February 1990.

tours.name: Rome on screen: real spots and fakes
tours.intro: Stand where the scene was shot, and learn what was faked: neorealism's real streets, Hollywood's replicas, Cinecittà's rebuilt Via Veneto.
tours.how: Centre on foot; Pigneto and EUR by metro.
story: Rossellini and De Sica shot on streets still full of rubble; Fellini rebuilt the city in the studio; Hollywood built St Peter's Square in California and the Spanish Steps in England. This tour separates the real from the set.

stops.note: Roma città aperta (1945): really here.
Ladri di biciclette (1948): the theft spot.
Roman Holiday (1953): the hand.
Roman Holiday: Joe's courtyard at no. 51.
Roman Holiday: the press conference.

Angels & Demons: the 'Vatican archive'.

tours.intro: Real places behind Goethe, Hawthorne, Henry James, Gadda and Morante.
tours.how: Centre on foot; Via Merulana and the Verano by tram.
story: Foreign writers came for the ruins and the Catholic strangeness; Italian writers wrote the modern city of crime and bombs.

The Marble Faun: Hilda's tower.
The Marble Faun: the dead Capuchin.
Daisy Miller's grave 'in an angle of the wall'.
Gadda's Pasticciaccio.

tours.name: Built for an event, then left
tours.intro: A world's fair that never opened, the 1960 Olympics, the 1990 World Cup, the 2009 swimming championships: what Rome built, and what it did with it afterwards.
tours.how: Flaminio on foot, EUR by metro, Tor Vergata by bus.
story: Rome keeps building for events and then leaving the buildings: a stadium closed since 2011, a velodrome blown up, a racecourse rotting, a sail that stood unfinished for fifteen years.

1960: the athletes' village and Nervi's viaduct.
1960: still in use.
1960: closed since 2011.

tours.name: Housing the poor: from borgate to megablocks
tours.intro: How Rome housed the people it pushed out of the centre: the Fascist borgate, the INA-Casa 'village', a walled kasbah, a kilometre-long slab and a ring of bridges.
tours.how: Outer districts; a day by metro and bus, or a bike.
story: From the 1930s the regime moved the poor from the demolished centre to borgate on the edge; after the war INA-Casa built humane villages; in the 1970s–80s the city went for megastructures that promised everything and delivered little.

stops.note: 1940–43: the last Fascist borgata.
1950–54: Libera's kasbah inside INA-Casa.
1970s–80s: a kilometre of concrete.
